questions.q: Find $\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&4\\5&6&0\end{bmatrix}$ by cofactor expansion along the first row.

questions.answer: $\det A=4-6=-2$, $\det B=6-0=6$, so $\det A\det B=-12$. $AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&7\\6&15\end{bmatrix}$, and $\det(AB)=2(15)-7(6)=30-42=-12$. They match.

questions.q: State the invertibility criterion in terms of the determinant.
questions.answer: A square matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det A\ne0$.

questions.q: Is $\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ invertible? Justify using the determinant.
questions.answer: $\det=2(2)-4(1)=0$. Since the determinant is $0$, the matrix is NOT invertible (singular).

questions.q: For what value(s) of $k$ is $\begin{bmatrix}k&2\\3&k\end{bmatrix}$ NOT invertible?
questions.answer: $\det=k^2-6$. Setting $k^2-6=0$ gives $k=\pm\sqrt6$. The matrix fails to be invertible exactly when $k=\sqrt6$ or $k=-\sqrt6$.

questions.q: Find $\det\begin{bmatrix}2&0&1\\3&1&2\\1&0&4\end{bmatrix}$ by expansion along the second column (it has two zeros).
questions.answer: Only $a_{22}=1$ is nonzero in column 2. $\det = 1\cdot\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&4\end{bmatrix} = 1(8-1)=7$. (Cross-check by expanding along row 1: $2\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&4\end{bmatrix}-0+1\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}=2(4)+1(-1)=7$. ✓)

questions.q: State the shortcut for the determinant of a triangular matrix (all entries above, or below, the main diagonal are zero).
questions.answer: The determinant equals the product of the diagonal entries.

questions.q: If you swap two rows of a matrix, how does the determinant change?
questions.answer: Its sign flips (multiplied by $-1$); the magnitude is unchanged.

questions.q: If a matrix has two identical rows, what must its determinant be, and why?
questions.answer: Swapping the two identical rows leaves the matrix unchanged but must flip the determinant's sign — the only number equal to its own negative is $0$, so the determinant must be $0$.

questions.q: The area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{u}=\langle a,b\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v}=\langle c,d\rangle$ equals $\left|\det\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}\right|$. Find the area for $\mathbf{u}=\langle3,1\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,4\rangle$.
For an $n\times n$ matrix $A$, $\det(cA)=c^n\det(A)$. If $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=2A$, find $\det(B)$ using this rule, then verify directly.

questions.answer: Triangular, so the determinant is the product of the diagonal: $(-2)(3)=-6$.

questions.q: Find $\det\begin{bmatrix}6&2\\3&1\end{bmatrix}$, and note what it tells you about invertibility.
questions.answer: $6(1)-2(3)=6-6=0$. The determinant is $0$, so this matrix is singular (not invertible) — its rows are proportional ($\langle6,2\rangle=2\langle3,1\rangle$).
